en.title: Data Science: the whole course
en.short: What data science is, how a degree is organised, the main areas in order, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Data science is the study of how to turn data into reliable knowledge and useful decisions. It combines statistics, computing and subject knowledge. The work includes collecting data, checking its quality, storing it, analysing it, explaining results and guarding privacy. Machine learning is one part of the field, not the whole of it.

A data scientist must reason about uncertainty. A result from a sample may not hold for the whole population. A model may fit past data and fail on new data. Good practice therefore joins coding with statistics, clear writing and knowledge of the area the data comes from, such as health, agriculture, finance or education.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc programme commonly runs for four years, and the National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum academic standards. The older Benchmark Minimum Academic Standards (BMAS) are being replaced by the Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS), so check which set applies to your intake. Some programmes include industrial training; check your department handbook for the weeks and timing. Nigerian master’s degrees commonly take one to two years, and awards include MSc and PGD.

In Ghana and Kenya, a first degree often takes four years. In England, a bachelor’s degree usually takes three years. In South Africa, a three-year BSc may be followed by an Honours year. Master’s programmes usually add advanced courses and a dissertation. These are common patterns only. Your own handbook is the authority on course lists, credit units, industrial training, project rules and graduation requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds foundations. You learn programming for data science, data types and measurement scales, data quality, descriptive statistics, probability, linear algebra, calculus and optimisation. You then practise data wrangling with spreadsheets and data libraries, relational databases and SQL, and exploratory data analysis with basic visualisation. These topics support everything later, so do not treat them as preliminary chores.

The core stage covers statistical inference, regression, experimental design and causal inference, classification and supervised learning, model evaluation and selection, feature engineering and preprocessing, unsupervised learning, time series and forecasting, text and natural language processing, data engineering and pipelines, big data and distributed computing, deep learning foundations, data visualisation and communication, ethics, privacy and governance, and the project lifecycle with a capstone. The order varies between institutions, and some topics may be options.

The master’s stage usually adds advanced statistical learning, Bayesian inference and probabilistic modelling, advanced deep learning, and research methods with a dissertation. A dissertation is a supervised research project. Check your programme for prerequisites and options.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Write code every week and work with real, messy data. Type the examples, change them and predict the output before you run them. Keep a notebook or script that starts from the raw file and ends with the result, so that another person can rerun it. Learn version control early.

Do the statistics by hand on small examples. For each method, learn the question it answers, the assumptions it makes and how to check them. When you fit a model, separate training data from test data before you look at the test results. Practise explaining a chart or model to a non-specialist in plain words. Follow your university’s rules on AI tools, and be able to explain every line you submit.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Common mistakes include:
Treating data science as only machine learning and skipping statistics.
Ignoring data quality, missing values and measurement scales.
Confusing correlation with causation.
Using test data during model building, which is data leakage.
Reporting training accuracy as if it were performance on new data.
Overfitting a model to noise, or choosing a complex model without a baseline.
Testing many hypotheses and reporting only the significant ones.
Making charts that mislead through truncated axes or poor scales.
Ignoring consent, privacy, bias and governance rules.
Leaving the capstone or dissertation late, with no time to test and write.

keyPoints: Data science combines statistics, computing and domain knowledge to turn data into reliable decisions.
Degrees and awards differ by country, so check your own handbook for length, industrial training and project rules.
Foundations in programming, statistics, probability and linear algebra support every later method.
Study by writing code weekly, working with messy data and checking assumptions by hand.
Separate training and test data, and do not confuse correlation with causation.
Ethics, privacy and clear communication are part of the work, not extras.

en.title: Programming for data science
en.short: Writing Python or R scripts to load, inspect and transform a small dataset.

sections.heading: Scripts and variables
sections.text: A script is a text file of instructions run in order. In Python or R, a variable is a name that refers to a value. Assignment stores a value: age = 21 in Python, age <- 21 in R. Names should be descriptive. Comments start with # in both languages and explain why code exists. A script should be reproducible: running it from top to bottom gives the same result.

sections.heading: Control flow and functions
Data structures and files
sections.text: Data structures hold several values. A list is an ordered sequence; a dictionary maps keys to values; a data frame is a table with named columns. In R, a vector is the basic sequence and a data frame is common. A CSV file stores rows as lines with columns separated by commas. Reading files: Python’s pandas library uses pandas.read_csv('scores.csv'); R uses read.csv('scores.csv'). Always inspect after loading: df.head(), df.shape, df.columns in pandas; head(df), dim(df), names(df) in R.

sections.heading: Libraries and example
sections.text: Libraries are collections of tested functions. Import pandas as pd, then df = pd.read_csv('scores.csv'). Inspect with df.head() and df.info(). Transform with df['pass'] = df['score'] >= 50. This creates a Boolean column. Summarise with df.groupby('class')['score'].mean(). Example: scores 40, 55, 70 give mean 55.0; pass flags False, True, True. Check results on a few rows before trusting a whole script.

keyPoints: Run scripts from top to bottom so results are reproducible.
A variable names a value; assignment stores it.
Control flow uses if, for and while to choose or repeat actions.
A function takes arguments and returns an output.
pandas.read_csv loads a CSV file into a data frame; inspect it with df.head() and df.shape.
df['pass'] = df['score'] >= 50 creates a Boolean column from a condition.

en.title: Data types, measurement scales and data quality
en.short: Structured and unstructured data, measurement scales, tidy layout, missing values and error sources.

sections.heading: Data types
sections.text: Structured data sits in rows and columns with a fixed schema, such as a table of student records. Unstructured data has no fixed table shape, such as free text, images or audio. Semi-structured data, such as JSON, has tags but no strict table. The type decides what tools you need: tables suit SQL and spreadsheets, while text needs parsing before counting words. It also affects storage and how easily you can join records.

sections.heading: Measurement scales
sections.text: A nominal scale labels categories with no order: blood group, city, yes/no. You can count frequencies but not average them. An ordinal scale has a meaningful order but unequal or unknown gaps: satisfaction low, medium, high. Medians and ranks are valid; means are often misleading. An interval scale has equal gaps but no true zero: temperature in °C. Differences are meaningful, ratios are not, so 20 °C is not twice 10 °C. A ratio scale has equal gaps and a true zero: age, income, study hours. Ratios are meaningful.

sections.heading: Tidy data and quality
sections.text: Tidy data has one row per observation, one column per variable and one table per type of observational unit. Example: a survey of 30 students should have one row per student and one column for each variable such as name, satisfaction and study hours. It is untidy to cram several answers into one cell or to spread one variable across several columns. Missing values are blanks or codes such as NA. They shrink the sample and can bias results if missingness relates to the value. Common errors include inconsistent units, duplicate rows, typos, impossible values and sampling only easy cases.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Scales limit later analysis. Nominal variables need counts or encoding; ordinal variables suit rank methods; interval and ratio variables allow means and standard deviations, but ratio variables also allow ratios. Poor quality carries through cleaning, modelling and reporting. Check types, units, ranges and missingness before analysis.

keyPoints: Structured data has a fixed row-and-column schema; unstructured data does not.
Nominal data labels categories, ordinal data has order, interval data has equal gaps, and ratio data has a true zero.
A nominal mean is meaningless; ordinal data is best summarised with medians or ranks.
Interval differences are meaningful but ratios are not; ratio scales allow ratios.
Tidy data has one row per observation, one column per variable and one table per type of observational unit.
Missing values and errors such as wrong units or duplicates can bias or break later analysis, so check them first.

en.title: Descriptive statistics
en.short: Centre, spread, frequency tables, correlation and summary tables for describing data before modelling.

sections.heading: Centre
sections.text:
Measures of centre give a typical value. The mean is Σx ÷ n, where Σ means sum and n is the number of observations. The median is the middle value after sorting; with an even n it is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the most frequent value.

The mean uses every value and is pulled by outliers; the median is more resistant.

sections.heading: Spread
sections.text:
Spread says how far values lie from the centre. Range is maximum − minimum. Variance is the average squared deviation; for a sample use s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1), and standard deviation is s = √s².

The interquartile range IQR = Q3 − Q1 covers the middle half. Report centre and spread together, because one without the other hides the shape.

sections.heading: Frequency and correlation
sections.text:
A frequency distribution groups values into class intervals and counts each class. Add relative frequency (count ÷ n) and cumulative frequency to see proportions and how many values lie below a limit. A histogram shows the shape: symmetric, skewed or with outliers.

Correlation measures linear association. Pearson r = Σ((x − x̄)(y − ȳ)) ÷ √(Σ(x − x̄)² Σ(y − ȳ)²), from −1 to 1. r near 0 means little linear association; correlation does not prove causation.

sections.heading: Tables and example
sections.text:
A summary table lists each variable with n, missing count, mean, median, standard deviation, minimum and maximum.

For 2, 4, 4, 6, 9: n = 5, mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Deviations are −3, −1, −1, 1, 4; squares sum to 28; s² = 28 ÷ 4 = 7; s = √7 ≈ 2.65; range = 9 − 2 = 7. Describe these facts before modelling, and check missing values and outliers.

keyPoints: Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle sorted value; mode is the most frequent value.
Sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) and standard deviation s = √s².
Range = maximum − minimum; IQR = Q3 − Q1.
A frequency table gives class counts, relative frequencies and cumulative frequencies.
Pearson correlation r lies from −1 to 1 and measures linear association only, not causation.
Summarise n, missing values, centre, spread, minimum and maximum before modelling.

en.title: Probability for data science
en.short: Random variables, distributions, conditional probability, Bayes, expectation and variance for inference.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text: A random variable maps each outcome of a random experiment to a number. A discrete random variable takes separate values, such as counts. Its probability mass function gives P(X = x). A continuous random variable takes values in an interval, and probabilities come from a probability density function: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the area under the curve. For any random variable, probabilities lie between 0 and 1 and sum or integrate to 1.

sections.heading: Distributions
sections.text: Common discrete distributions are Bernoulli (one trial, success probability p), binomial (number of successes in n independent trials), and Poisson (counts of rare events in a fixed interval, mean λ). The uniform distribution gives equal density over an interval. The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, fixed by mean μ and variance σ²; many sums and averages are approximately normal. These models are building blocks for likelihoods and machine learning assumptions.

sections.heading: Conditional probability
sections.text: Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B), with P(B) > 0. Events are independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Bayes’ theorem reverses a conditional: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A) ÷ P(B). Here P(A) is the prior, P(B | A) the likelihood, and P(A | B) the posterior. This update rule underlies Bayesian inference and classifiers such as naive Bayes.

sections.heading: Expectation and variance
sections.text: Expectation E(X) is the long-run mean: Σ x P(X = x) for discrete X. Variance Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − μ² measures spread; its square root is the standard deviation. If X is Bernoulli with p = 0.3, E(X) = 0.3 and Var(X) = p(1 − p) = 0.21. For independent X and Y, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Expectation and variance summarise distributions and appear in loss functions, estimators and model uncertainty.

keyPoints: Random variables give numerical values to outcomes; discrete ones use a probability mass function and continuous ones a density.
Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).
Bayes’ theorem: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A) ÷ P(B).
Expectation is the long-run mean; variance is E[(X − μ)²] = E(X²) − μ².
For a Bernoulli variable with success probability p, E(X) = p and Var(X) = p(1 − p).
Independent variables add variances: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y).

en.title: Linear algebra for data science
en.short: Vectors, matrices, products, transpose, inverse, rank and eigenvectors, with data examples.

sections.heading: Vectors as data
sections.text: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. A row of a data table can be a vector of features; a column can be one variable. The dot product is u·v = Σ uᵢvᵢ. It measures alignment and underlies linear models. The length of u is √(u·u). A simple score is y = w·x + b, with weight vector w and feature vector x.

sections.heading: Matrices and products
sections.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array. An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. A data matrix X often has rows as observations and columns as features. Matrix multiplication C = AB needs A to be m × k and B to be k × n; then C is m × n and cᵢⱼ = Σₚ aᵢₚ bₚⱼ. Order matters: AB is usually not BA.

Example: A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], B = [[1, 0], [2, 1]]. AB = [[5, 2], [11, 4]] and BA = [[1, 2], [5, 8]], so AB ≠ BA.

sections.heading: Transpose, inverse, rank
sections.text: The transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns. The inverse A⁻¹ satisfies A A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ A = I, where I is the identity matrix. Only square matrices can have an inverse, and many do not. The rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its rank equals its size. In regression, XᵀX and its inverse appear in the normal equations, but software avoids forming the inverse directly.

sections.heading: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
sections.text:
A nonzero vector v is an eigenvector of a square matrix A when Av = λv, where λ is its eigenvalue. The vector is mapped to a scalar multiple of itself. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors help describe variance directions in data, as in principal component analysis.

Example: A = [[2, 0], [0, 3]]. For v = (1, 0), Av = (2, 0) = 2v, so λ = 2. For v = (0, 1), Av = (0, 3) = 3v, so λ = 3.

keyPoints: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; the dot product is u·v = Σ uᵢvᵢ.
A data matrix has rows as observations and columns as features.
For C = AB, cᵢⱼ = Σₚ aᵢₚ bₚⱼ, and AB is usually not BA.
The transpose swaps rows and columns; A A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ A = I for an invertible square matrix.
Rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns; a square matrix is invertible exactly when rank equals size.
A nonzero eigenvector satisfies Av = λv; eigenvalues and eigenvectors give variance directions in methods such as principal component analysis.

en.title: Calculus and optimisation basics
en.short: Functions, derivatives, gradients, maxima and minima, and gradient descent for fitting models.

sections.heading: Functions and derivatives
sections.text: A function maps an input to an output. In data science the input is often a parameter and the output a loss, a number that measures how badly a model fits. The derivative f′(x) gives the slope of f at x: how fast the output changes when x changes slightly. A zero derivative marks a flat point. For f(x)=x²−4x+1, f′(x)=2x−4. Setting 2x−4=0 gives x=2, and f(2)=−3. Since f″(x)=2>0, this point is a minimum.

sections.heading: Partial derivatives and gradients
sections.text: A partial derivative measures the slope along one variable while the others stay fixed. For f(x,y)=x²+3y², ∂f/∂x=2x and ∂f/∂y=6y. The gradient is the vector of all partial derivatives: ∇f=(2x,6y). It points in the direction of steepest increase. At (0,0) the gradient is (0,0), and f has its minimum there.

sections.heading: Maxima and minima
sections.text: A maximum is a point higher than nearby points; a minimum is lower. In one variable, solve f′(x)=0 and check the second derivative: f″>0 means a minimum, f″<0 means a maximum. In several variables, set every partial derivative to zero and check the Hessian matrix, the table of second partial derivatives. Some flat points are neither maxima nor minima.

sections.heading: Gradient descent
sections.text: Gradient descent finds a minimum by repeated steps. Start at a point, compute the gradient, and move a small distance opposite it: xnew = x − α ∇f(x). The learning rate α controls step size. Too large and the steps overshoot; too small and convergence is slow. Example: minimise f(x)=x² from x=1 with α=0.1. The derivative is 2x, so the next x is 1 − 0.1×2 = 0.8; the next is 0.8 − 0.1×1.6 = 0.64. The values approach 0. Fitting a model means choosing parameters that minimise a loss, so this loop is the basic engine of many training algorithms.

keyPoints: A derivative f′(x) gives the slope of a function and is zero at a flat point.
A partial derivative ∂f/∂x gives the slope along x while other variables stay fixed.
The gradient ∇f is the vector of partial derivatives and points toward steepest increase.
For one variable, f′(x)=0 with f″>0 gives a minimum; f″<0 gives a maximum.
Gradient descent updates xnew = x − α ∇f(x), where α is the learning rate.
Model fitting minimises a loss over parameters, so gradients and gradient descent are central.

en.title: Data wrangling with spreadsheets and data libraries
en.short: Cleaning, reshaping, filtering, joining and aggregating tables, with missing values and tidy data.

sections.heading: Tidy tables
sections.text: Tidy data has a simple shape: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit forms one table. A variable is a measured property; an observation is one case. This shape makes filtering, joining and aggregating predictable. A wide table with a column for each month is often not tidy, because month is a variable hidden in the column names.

sections.heading: Cleaning and missing values
sections.text:
Cleaning starts with consistent types and labels: trim stray spaces, use one spelling for each category, store numbers as numbers, and remove exact duplicate rows. In a spreadsheet, filters and remove-duplicates help; a library such as pandas uses boolean masks and string methods.

Missing values need an explicit rule. A blank cell may mean zero, not recorded, or not applicable. Decide whether to drop the row, fill with a stated value, or keep a missing marker and report the count. Never silently replace blanks with zero. Document the choice.

sections.heading: Filter, join, aggregate
sections.text:
Filtering keeps rows that meet a condition. Joining matches rows from two tables on a key, such as a product code. Aggregating groups rows and computes a summary, such as a sum or mean. A spreadsheet pivot table groups and aggregates; a library uses groupby.

Example: sales rows (P1, 10), (P2, 5), (P1, 7), (P3, 4) join to products P1 Tools, P2 Tools, P3 Garden. Group by category and sum quantity: Tools = 10 + 5 + 7 = 22; Garden = 4. Tools has 3 rows, so its mean is 22 ÷ 3 = 7.33 (2 decimal places). Check row counts before and after a join; a wrong key can duplicate rows.

sections.heading: Reshaping
sections.text: Reshaping changes layout, not the data. Wide data puts months in separate columns. Long data has a month column and a value column, which is often tidy because month is a variable. Pivot longer and pivot wider convert between the two. Keep names clear and check that totals are unchanged after reshaping.

keyPoints: Tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each unit is one table.
Missing values must be explicit: decide to drop, fill, or flag, and document it.
Filtering keeps rows; joining matches rows on a key; aggregation summarises groups.
Check row counts before and after a join because a wrong key can duplicate rows.
Reshaping changes layout, not values; wide and long forms can hold the same data.
In the example, Tools total is 22 with mean 7.33, and Garden total is 4.

en.title: Relational databases and SQL
en.short: Tables, keys, SELECT queries, joins, aggregation and basic schema design for relational databases.

sections.heading: Tables and keys
sections.text: A relational database stores data in tables, also called relations. Each row (tuple) is one record; each column (attribute) holds one kind of value. A primary key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL. A foreign key is a column that refers to a primary key in another table, linking the tables. Example: Students(student_id, name, dept_id) and Departments(dept_id, dept_name). student_id is the primary key of Students; dept_id is a foreign key to Departments.

sections.heading: SELECT queries
sections.text: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases, though dialects differ. A basic query is SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition. WHERE filters rows before grouping. ORDER BY sorts the result. Example: SELECT name FROM Students WHERE dept_id = 1 ORDER BY name; returns Ada, Bola, Efe from the sample below. Use * for all columns. NULL means unknown or missing; comparisons with NULL need IS NULL, not = NULL.

sections.heading: Joins
sections.text: A join combines rows from two tables using a related column. INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match in both tables. LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table and fills unmatched right columns with NULL. Example: SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM Students s INNER JOIN Departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id; lists each student with the department name.

sections.heading: Aggregation and design
sections.text: Aggregate functions summarise many rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY makes one group per distinct value; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Sample data: Departments(1 Physics, 2 Chemistry, 3 Maths); Students(101 Ada 1, 102 Bola 1, 103 Chidi 2, 104 Dayo 3, 105 Efe 1). Query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM Students s JOIN Departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; returns Physics, 3. For schema design, start from entities and relationships, give each table a primary key, use foreign keys, and normalise. First normal form needs atomic values; second removes partial dependency on part of a composite key; third removes transitive dependency.

keyPoints: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL; a foreign key refers to a primary key in another table.
A SELECT query names columns, a FROM table and an optional WHERE condition; ORDER BY sorts the result.
INNER JOIN keeps only matching rows, while LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows and fills missing right values with NULL.
GROUP BY groups rows for aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG; HAVING filters the groups.
Normalise tables to at least third normal form to reduce redundancy and update anomalies.
Test queries on small sample data and handle NULL with IS NULL, not = NULL.

en.title: Exploratory data analysis and basic visualisation
en.short: Summary statistics, distributions, relationships, outlier checks and choosing honest basic charts.

sections.heading: Exploring one variable
sections.text:
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) means looking at a dataset before modelling: its shape, centre, spread and unusual values. Summary statistics describe these: the mean is the average, the median is the middle value when sorted (or the average of the two middle values if the count is even), and the standard deviation measures spread around the mean. The distribution shows which values are common. A histogram groups numeric values into bins; a box plot shows median, quartiles and possible outliers. Check outliers with a rule of thumb such as below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR, where IQR = Q3 − Q1. Investigate, do not delete automatically.

Example: 2, 4, 4, 5, 15. Sum = 30, mean = 30 ÷ 5 = 6, median = 4. The value 15 pulls the mean up, so report both.

sections.heading: Relationships and overplotting
sections.text: For two numeric variables, use a scatter plot and look for direction, form and strength. Correlation r, from −1 to 1, measures linear association only; r near 0 does not prove no relationship. For a numeric variable by category, use side-by-side box plots or a bar chart of group means. For two categories, use a contingency table or grouped bars. Overplotting happens when many points overlap and hide density. Reduce it with smaller points, transparency (alpha), jitter for repeated values, or binning such as a hexbin plot.

sections.heading: Honest charts
sections.text: Choose charts by data type and question. One numeric variable: histogram or box plot. One categorical variable: bar chart of counts or proportions. Two numeric variables: scatter plot. Values over time: line chart. Bar charts should start at zero because their length encodes size. A truncated y-axis can exaggerate small differences; label axes, units and sample size. Avoid 3D effects, unnecessary colour and pie charts with many slices. A good chart answers one clear question.

keyPoints: EDA checks centre, spread, distribution, relationships and outliers before modelling.
Mean = sum ÷ n; median is the middle sorted value (average of the two middle values if n is even) and resists outliers.
IQR = Q3 − Q1; flag values below Q1 − 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR for review.
Correlation r = Σ((x−x̄)(y−ȳ)) ÷ √(Σ(x−x̄)² Σ(y−ȳ)²) measures linear association only.
Match chart to data: histogram or box plot for one numeric, bar chart for categories, scatter for two numeric, line for time.
Start bar charts at zero, label axes, and reduce overplotting with transparency, jitter or binning.

en.title: Statistical inference
en.short: Sampling distributions, the central limit theorem, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, p-values and errors.

sections.heading: Sampling distributions
sections.text:
A statistic such as the sample mean is a random variable: it varies from sample to sample. Its sampling distribution is its distribution over repeated samples of size n. For a mean with population standard deviation σ, the standard error is SE = σ/√n. It measures variation between samples, not spread within the data.

The central limit theorem says the sample mean is roughly normal for large n, whatever the population shape, if observations are independent and σ is finite.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals
sections.text:
A 95% confidence interval for μ is x̄ ± 1.96 × SE; the 1.96 leaves 2.5% in each tail. Use a t value when σ is estimated from the sample.

Example: n = 100, x̄ = 52.0, σ = 10, so SE = 10 ÷ √100 = 1.0. The interval is 52.0 ± 1.96, that is 50.04 to 53.96.

Read it correctly: over repeated sampling, about 95% of such intervals would contain μ. It is not a 95% probability that μ lies in this one interval.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests and errors
sections.text:
A test sets a null hypothesis H0 against an alternative H1. The test statistic measures how far the data fall from H0 in standard error units. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed, assuming H0 is true.

Here H0: μ = 50 gives z = (52.0 − 50) ÷ 1.0 = 2.0. The two-sided p-value is about 0.046, so at the 5% level we reject H0. A Type I error rejects a true H0, at rate α; a Type II error fails to reject a false H0, and one minus its rate is the power.

sections.heading: What inference cannot do
sections.text: Inference supports population claims only if the sample is drawn properly and the model is roughly right. It cannot prove H0 true; a p-value is not the probability that H0 is true. A small p-value does not mean a large effect, and observational data alone do not establish causation.

keyPoints: The standard error of a sample mean is SE = σ/√n, and it describes variation between samples, not within one sample.
The central limit theorem makes the sample mean roughly normal for large n, so normal-based intervals and tests work even for skewed populations.
A 95% confidence interval is x̄ ± 1.96 × SE; it describes the procedure, not the probability that μ lies inside one interval.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true; it is not the probability that H0 is true.
A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis at rate α; a Type II error misses a false one, and power is 1 minus that rate.
Inference needs a proper sample and a roughly correct model, and it cannot by itself show that an effect is large or causal.

en.title: Regression analysis
en.short: Fitting, checking and reporting simple and multiple linear regression models.

sections.heading: The model
sections.text: Simple linear regression models a numeric response y as y = β0 + β1x + ε. β0 is the intercept, β1 the slope, and ε the error term. Multiple regression extends this to y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βpxp + ε. Each coefficient is the expected change in y for a one-unit increase in its predictor, holding the other predictors fixed. This holding-fixed wording is essential in multiple regression. Association is not causation unless the design supports it.

sections.heading: Least squares
sections.text: Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals, SSE = Σ(yi − ŷi)². For simple regression, b1 = Sxy ÷ Sxx and b0 = ȳ − b1x̄, where Sxy = Σ(xi − x̄)(yi − ȳ) and Sxx = Σ(xi − x̄)². Example: for five students, x = hours studied = 1,2,3,4,5 and y = exam score = 2,4,5,4,5. x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4, Sxx = 10, Sxy = 6, so b1 = 0.6 and b0 = 2.2. The fitted line is ŷ = 2.2 + 0.6x. R² = 1 − SSE ÷ SST = 1 − 2.4 ÷ 6 = 0.6.

sections.heading: Assumptions and checks
sections.text: Standard inference assumes linearity, independent errors, constant error variance (homoscedasticity), and normally distributed errors. It also assumes no severe multicollinearity and no highly influential points. Plot residuals against fitted values for linearity and constant variance. A normal Q-Q plot checks normality. Residuals against leverage or Cook’s distance flag influence. Variance inflation factors (VIFs) flag multicollinearity. These checks guide model changes; they do not prove the model correct.

sections.heading: Reporting
sections.text: Report the fitted equation, coefficient estimates with standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values, plus R² and the residual standard error. State the sample size and how variables were measured. Describe diagnostic checks and any changes. Avoid causal language unless justified. In the example, report b1 = 0.6 with its software confidence interval and R² = 0.6, then say each extra hour is associated with 0.6 points higher score in this sample.

keyPoints: Simple linear regression is y = β0 + β1x + ε; multiple regression adds more predictors.
Least squares chooses coefficients that minimise SSE = Σ(yi − ŷi)².
In simple regression, b1 = Sxy ÷ Sxx and b0 = ȳ − b1x̄.
A coefficient gives the change in y per one-unit increase in its predictor, holding the others fixed.
Check linearity and constant variance with residuals versus fitted, normality with a Q-Q plot, influence with leverage or Cook’s distance, and collinearity with VIFs.
Report estimates, standard errors, confidence intervals, R² and residual standard error, and avoid causal claims without design support.

en.title: Experimental design and causal inference
en.short: Randomised trials, confounding, observational versus experimental data, potential outcomes and DAGs.

sections.heading: Why causality is hard
sections.text:
An association is not automatically causal. A treatment may appear to help because those who receive it differ from those who do not.

In a Kano clinic, patients given a malaria drug may recover faster because they are younger or less poor. Age and income are confounders: they affect both treatment and outcome. Observational data record treatment as it happens. Experimental data come from a design where the researcher controls assignment.

sections.heading: Randomised trials
sections.text:
A randomised controlled trial (RCT) assigns treatment by chance. Randomisation tends to balance measured and unmeasured confounders, so outcome differences can be attributed to treatment.

In the Kano example, random assignment avoids doctors giving the drug to healthier patients. Blinding reduces bias, and intention-to-treat analysis compares groups as randomised. RCTs can still fail through chance imbalance in small samples, poor compliance, or unrealistic settings. They are not always ethical or practical.

sections.heading: Potential outcomes
sections.text:
For each person define Y(1) as the outcome with treatment and Y(0) without it. The individual effect is Y(1) − Y(0), but we never see both for the same person. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference.

The average treatment effect is ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)]. In an RCT, the difference in mean outcomes between treated and control groups estimates the ATE. In observational data, that difference estimates the ATE only if treatment is independent of potential outcomes given measured confounders, an untestable assumption.

sections.heading: DAGs and backdoors
sections.text:
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) draws variables as nodes and causal effects as arrows, with no cycles. A backdoor path is a non-causal path from treatment to outcome.

To estimate a causal effect, block every backdoor path by adjusting for confounders. Do not adjust for a collider, a variable affected by both treatment and outcome, because that can create bias. Do not adjust for a mediator unless you want a direct effect. Treat a relationship as causal only when design or assumptions justify it, not merely because a model fits.

keyPoints: Randomisation balances confounders in expectation, so an RCT can estimate a causal effect.
Confounding occurs when a variable affects both treatment and outcome.
Potential outcomes Y(1) and Y(0) cannot both be observed for one person; the average treatment effect is ATE = E[Y(1) − Y(0)].
In observational data, a treatment-outcome association is causal only under assumptions such as no unmeasured confounding.
In a DAG, block backdoor paths by adjusting for confounders, but do not adjust for colliders or mediators.
Treat a relationship as causal only when the design or stated assumptions justify it, not just because a model fits.

en.title: Classification and supervised learning
en.short: Logistic regression, kNN, decision trees, random forests and naive Bayes, with training and comparison.

sections.heading: Logistic regression
sections.text: Logistic regression models a binary class probability. It forms z = β0 + β1x1 + ... and returns p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−z). Training fits the β values by maximum likelihood, which maximises the probability of the observed labels. The output is a probability, so a threshold such as 0.5 gives a class. Example: β0 = −2, β1 = 1, x = 3 gives z = 1 and p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−1) = 0.731, so the class is 1.

sections.heading: Neighbours and trees
sections.text:
k-nearest neighbours (kNN) stores the training data. To classify a new point, it finds the k closest training points, usually by Euclidean distance, and takes a majority vote. It has no real training step, but prediction is slow on large data and feature scaling matters.

A decision tree asks yes/no questions about feature thresholds. Training picks splits that reduce impurity, such as Gini impurity or entropy. A small tree is easy to read; a deep tree can overfit.

A random forest trains many trees on bootstrap samples and random feature subsets, then votes. This usually reduces the variance of one tree but makes the model harder to interpret.

sections.heading: Naive Bayes
sections.text: Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ theorem: p(C|x) ∝ p(C) × Π p(xi|C). It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class. That assumption is often false, but the method is fast and works well for text. Training estimates class priors and feature probabilities from counts or distributions.

sections.heading: Comparing classifiers
sections.text: Compare classifiers on data not used for training, with the same splits and protocol. Report a confusion matrix and choose metrics that match costs, such as precision and recall. Also consider calibration, interpretability, training time and data size. No classifier is best everywhere; test on your problem.

keyPoints: Logistic regression returns p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^−z) with z = β0 + β1x1 + ... and is trained by maximum likelihood.
kNN classifies by majority vote among the k nearest training points and has no real training step.
Decision trees split on feature thresholds to reduce impurity such as Gini impurity or entropy.
Random forests vote over many trees trained on bootstrap samples and random feature subsets, reducing variance.
Naive Bayes uses p(C|x) ∝ p(C) × Π p(xi|C) and assumes conditional independence of features.
Compare classifiers on held-out data with the same splits, using metrics and costs that fit the problem.

en.title: Model evaluation and selection
en.short: Train, validation and test splits, cross-validation, metrics, bias-variance and tuning.

sections.heading: Splits and cross-validation
sections.text: Split data into training, validation and test sets. Fit on training data, choose settings on validation data, and use the test set once for the final estimate. A 60/20/20 split is common; small datasets need cross-validation. In k-fold cross-validation, divide the training data into k folds, train on k−1 and validate on the last, then average the k scores. Use stratified folds for classification. For time series, split by time and never train on the future.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text:
Classification uses the confusion matrix: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), true negatives (TN). Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ N. Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP). Recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN). F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall). Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data. Regression uses MAE = Σ|y − ŷ| ÷ n, RMSE = √(Σ(y − ŷ)² ÷ n) and R².

Example: TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 45.
Accuracy = 85 ÷ 100 = 0.85
Precision = 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80
Recall = 40 ÷ 45 = 0.889
F1 = 80 ÷ 95 = 0.842

sections.heading: Bias, variance and tuning
sections.text: Bias is error from an overly simple model; variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample. As complexity rises, bias falls and variance rises. The best model balances them by minimising validation error. Hyperparameters are settings chosen before fitting, such as tree depth or regularisation strength. Tune them by grid or random search using validation scores or cross-validation. Nested cross-validation gives a less optimistic estimate when tuning and reporting together.

sections.heading: Honest reporting
sections.text: Overfitting means learning noise, so training scores look good but test scores do not. Avoid data leakage: do not use test data in preprocessing, feature selection or tuning. Report the test result once, with the metric chosen in advance. Show a baseline and for classification more than accuracy. Keep the split fixed.

keyPoints: Use training data to fit, validation data to tune, and the test set once for the final estimate.
In k-fold cross-validation, average the scores from k held-out folds; stratify folds for classification.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) ÷ N; precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP); recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN); F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall).
For regression, MAE = Σ|y − ŷ| ÷ n, RMSE = √(Σ(y − ŷ)² ÷ n) and R² = 1 − SSres ÷ SStot; RMSE penalises large errors more.
The bias-variance trade-off means validation error is high when a model is too simple or too flexible.
Tune hyperparameters on validation or cross-validation scores, then report the untouched test score; never tune on the test set.

en.title: Feature engineering and preprocessing
en.short: Scaling, encoding, imputation, feature selection and leakage control in preprocessing.

sections.heading: Scaling and encoding
sections.text:
Feature scaling puts numeric variables on comparable ranges. Standardisation replaces x by z = (x − mean) ÷ sd, where sd is the standard deviation. Min-max scaling maps values to [0,1] with (x − min) ÷ (max − min). Distance-based and regularised models are sensitive to scale; tree models usually are not. Categorical variables need numeric encoding. One-hot encoding makes one column per category. Ordinal encoding uses ordered integers only when the order is real. Categories with many levels need care.

Example: two people differ by 10 years in age and 40,000 in income. Raw Euclidean distance is √(10² + 40,000²) ≈ 40,000, dominated by income. If age sd is 5 and income sd is 20,000, the standardised differences are 2 and 2, so distance is √(2² + 2²) = 2.83.

sections.heading: Imputation and leakage
sections.text:
Imputation fills missing values. Mean or median imputation is simple but shrinks variance; model-based imputation uses other columns. Missingness itself can be informative, so add a missing indicator. Data leakage happens when information from outside the training data, or from the target, enters preprocessing. Fit imputation, scaling and encoding on the training data only, then apply them to validation and test data. Split the data before preprocessing. Leakage makes test scores look better than they will be in use.

For example, scaling all rows before splitting uses the test mean and sd. That is leakage. The model has seen test information.

sections.heading: Selection and fairness
sections.text:
Feature selection keeps useful variables and drops noisy or redundant ones. Filter methods rank variables by simple statistics. Wrapper methods search subsets using model performance. Embedded methods select during training, for example L1 regularisation. Do selection inside cross-validation, or it leaks.

Preprocessing also affects fairness. A proxy variable, an indirect stand-in such as postcode or school, can carry group information. Imputation can distort minority patterns. Scaling choices can change group-level errors. Report performance by group and document preprocessing choices.

keyPoints: Fit scaling, imputation and encoding on the training data only, then apply them to validation and test data.
Standardisation uses z = (x − mean) ÷ sd; min-max scaling uses (x − min) ÷ (max − min).
Use one-hot encoding for unordered categories and ordinal encoding only when the order is real.
Impute missing values and consider adding a missing indicator when missingness may be informative.
Do feature selection inside cross-validation so that selection does not leak test information.
Check model errors by group because proxies, imputation and scaling can affect fairness.

en.title: Unsupervised learning: clustering, PCA and anomalies
en.short: k-means and hierarchical clustering, PCA, anomaly detection, and how to validate them without labels.

sections.heading: Clustering with k-means
sections.text:
Unsupervised learning finds structure without a target label. k-means partitions n points into k groups by minimising the within-cluster sum of squares, Σ over clusters Σ over points ||x − μ||², where μ is a cluster mean. It alternates assignment and mean update until stable. Standardise features first, because distance depends on scale. Choose k with domain knowledge and internal indices such as the silhouette score, which measures how well each point fits its cluster (higher is better).

Example: points (1,1), (2,1), (8,8), (9,8), k = 2, initial means (1,1), (9,8). One update gives means (1.5,1), (8.5,8); objective = 4 × 0.25 = 1.0.

sections.heading: Hierarchical clustering
sections.text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with each point as a cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair. Linkage defines closeness: single uses nearest points, complete uses farthest, average uses mean distance, and Ward minimises within-cluster variance. A dendrogram shows merge order; cutting it at a chosen height gives clusters. It needs no k in advance, but needs O(n²) memory and typically O(n²) to O(n³) time, and linkage choice changes the result.

sections.heading: Principal components
sections.text: Principal component analysis (PCA) builds orthogonal axes, called components, ordered by variance. Standardise each variable, z = (x − mean) ÷ standard deviation, then use the covariance or correlation matrix. The first component points in the direction of greatest variance; its eigenvalue is that variance. A scree plot and cumulative explained variance help choose how many components to keep. Loadings show variable contributions. PCA is linear and variance-focused, so it can miss nonlinear structure and is sensitive to scaling.

sections.heading: Anomalies and limits
sections.text: Anomaly detection flags points unlike the rest. Scores include distance to a centroid, local density, or reconstruction error after PCA. A threshold sets the expected contamination rate, the share of points flagged as anomalies, so validate with domain experts and stability checks. Without labels, accuracy cannot be measured; use internal indices, resampling, and whether clusters or components support a real question. k-means assumes roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters and is sensitive to outliers and initialisation. All unsupervised results are descriptive, not proof of causes.

keyPoints: k-means minimises Σ over clusters Σ over points ||x − μ||² and needs scaled features and a chosen k.
Hierarchical clustering merges closest clusters using a linkage rule; a dendrogram cut gives clusters.
PCA standardises z = (x − mean) ÷ sd and orders orthogonal components by eigenvalue, which equals explained variance.
Anomaly scores such as distance to a centroid or PCA reconstruction error need a threshold and domain validation.
Without labels, use internal indices such as the silhouette score, stability under resampling, and domain sense, not accuracy.
Unsupervised methods describe structure; they do not prove causes, and results depend on scaling, linkage or k, and outliers.

en.title: Time series and forecasting
en.short: Trend, seasonality, stationarity, autocorrelation, ARIMA and time-ordered backtesting.

sections.heading: Trend and seasonality
sections.text:
A time series is data in time order. Trend is slow change in level. Seasonality repeats at a fixed period. Noise is the rest. Plot first: trend calls for differencing; seasonality calls for seasonal differencing or seasonal terms. Differencing replaces each value with its change from the previous value; seasonal differencing subtracts the value one season earlier.

Example: quarterly sales 100, 120, 90, 110, 110, 132, 99, 121. Year two is 10 per cent higher each quarter, so trend is upward. Quarterly averages are 105, 126, 94.5 and 115.5. Against the overall mean 110.25, seasonal indices are 0.95, 1.14, 0.86 and 1.05 (rounded).

sections.heading: Stationarity and autocorrelation
sections.text:
A stationary series has constant mean and variance, with autocovariance depending only on the lag. ARIMA assumes stationarity after differencing. The autocorrelation function (ACF) gives correlation between y_t and y_(t−k) at lag k. Slow decay suggests trend; a spike at lag m suggests seasonality.

The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) removes shorter lags. Use ACF and PACF plots, and a test such as augmented Dickey-Fuller, to choose d.

sections.heading: ARIMA models
sections.text:
ARIMA(p,d,q) combines autoregression AR(p), differencing d times, and a moving average MA(q). With backshift B y_t = y_(t−1), the model is φ(B)(1−B)^d y_t = c + θ(B) ε_t, where ε_t is white noise, meaning uncorrelated random shocks.

p is the number of lagged values, q the number of lagged errors, and d the number of differences. Seasonal ARIMA adds seasonal terms, written (p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_m, where m is the seasonal period. Choose terms by plots, information criteria (penalised fit measures) and forecast performance.

sections.heading: Backtesting forecasts
sections.text:
Time order changes validation. A random train-test split lets the model learn from the future, which is leakage. Train on the past and test on later data.

In rolling-origin backtesting, fit up to time t, forecast the next h points, record the error, move t forward, and repeat. Use an expanding or fixed window. Compare with a naive forecast, such as the last value or last season. Report mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) or mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), and state the horizon. Multi-step errors are larger than one-step errors.

keyPoints: Trend is slow change in level; seasonality repeats at a fixed period; differencing removes trend and seasonal differencing removes a repeating pattern.
A stationary series has constant mean and variance, with autocovariance depending only on the lag; the ACF and PACF help choose differencing and ARIMA orders.
ARIMA(p,d,q) is φ(B)(1−B)^d y_t = c + θ(B) ε_t, with B y_t = y_(t−1), p autoregressive lags, d differences and q moving-average error lags.
Time order means training data must come before test data; a random split leaks future information.
Rolling-origin backtesting fits up to time t, forecasts h steps ahead, then moves t forward and repeats.
Compare forecasts with a naive baseline and report MAE, RMSE or MAPE for a stated horizon.

en.title: Text and natural language processing
en.short: Tokenisation, stop words, bag-of-words, TF-IDF, embeddings, text classification, sentiment, evaluation and bias.

sections.heading: Text to features
sections.text: Tokenisation splits text into tokens: words, subwords or characters. Word tokens are simple but struggle with punctuation, contractions and languages without spaces. Subword tokenisation (for example byte-pair encoding) handles unseen words. Stop words are very common words such as 'the' and 'is'. Removing them shrinks the vocabulary but can delete negation ('not good'), so test whether it helps your task. Bag-of-words represents a document as counts of each vocabulary word, ignoring order. It is simple and sparse but loses word order and context.

sections.heading: TF-IDF
sections.text:
TF-IDF weights a term by how often it occurs in a document (tf) and how rare it is across documents (idf). A common form is tf-idf(t,d) = tf(t,d) × log10(N ÷ df(t)), where N is the number of documents and df(t) is the number of documents containing t. Variants add smoothing.

Example: N = 3, term 'data' appears in 2 documents, and 3 times in one document.
idf = log10(3 ÷ 2) = 0.176
tf-idf = 3 × 0.176 = 0.528

Terms in every document get idf = 0.

sections.heading: Embeddings and classifiers
sections.text: Word embeddings map words to dense vectors learned from context, so similar words are close (word2vec, GloVe, fastText). They capture similarity but can encode stereotypes. For text classification, convert documents to vectors (bag-of-words, TF-IDF or averaged embeddings) and train a classifier. Sentiment analysis labels text as positive, negative or neutral. It can use a sentiment lexicon or supervised learning. Negation, sarcasm and domain words cause errors.

sections.heading: Evaluation and bias
sections.text: Evaluate on held-out data with accuracy, precision, recall and F1; for multiclass report macro or micro averages and a confusion matrix. Text data carries bias: sampling bias (who is represented), label bias (annotator judgement), historical bias (language reflects stereotypes) and representation bias (dialects and languages missing). Check per-group performance and inspect errors before deployment.

keyPoints: TF-IDF: tf-idf(t,d) = tf(t,d) × log10(N ÷ df(t)), with smoothing variants.
Bag-of-words counts words and ignores order; word embeddings give dense context-based vectors.
Stop-word removal can delete negation, so test it on your task.
Evaluate text classifiers on held-out data with precision, recall and F1, not accuracy alone.
Text data can carry sampling, label, historical and representation bias; check per-group errors.

en.title: Data engineering and pipelines
en.short: ETL, APIs, storage, orchestration, data versioning and pipeline testing for reproducible analysis.

sections.heading: ETL and APIs
sections.text: Extract, transform and load (ETL) is a pattern for moving data. Extract reads from sources such as files, databases or APIs. An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for software to request data, often over HTTP; good clients handle pagination, rate limits and errors. Transform cleans, validates, reshapes and joins data. Load writes the result to storage. Some systems load raw data first and transform later, called ELT; the choice depends on the warehouse.

sections.heading: Storage and orchestration
sections.text: Storage may be files such as CSV or Parquet, a relational database, an analytics warehouse, or a data lake for raw and varied data. Choose based on access patterns, schema needs and cost. Workflow orchestration runs tasks in a directed acyclic graph (DAG): tasks have dependencies and no cycles. The orchestrator schedules runs, retries failures, records logs and alerts. This makes daily loads repeatable rather than manual.

sections.heading: Versioning and testing
sections.text: Data versioning records the data snapshot, code commit and configuration that produced each output. Keep raw data immutable and write new versions instead of overwriting. Pipeline tests include unit tests for transform functions, schema checks, data quality assertions such as no null patient_id, and integration tests on a small sample. Test idempotency: rerunning a load must not duplicate rows. These controls catch errors before bad data reaches analysis.

sections.heading: Reproducible case
sections.text: Amina builds a clinic pipeline. It extracts appointment records from an API, transforms dates to ISO format and standardises phone numbers, then loads a warehouse table keyed by appointment_id. A test checks that appointment_date is not in the future and patient_id is present. The team versions the code commit, configuration and raw snapshot. Tunde can rerun the pipeline and rebuild the same feature table for a model, so his reported accuracy can be traced to exact inputs.

keyPoints: ETL extracts from sources, transforms and validates data, then loads it to storage.
An API is a defined interface for requesting data; clients must handle pagination, rate limits and errors.
A workflow orchestrator runs tasks in a DAG, managing dependencies, retries, logs and alerts.
Data versioning ties each output to a data snapshot, code commit and configuration.
Pipeline tests include unit tests, schema checks, data quality assertions, integration tests and idempotency checks.
Reproducible pipelines let analysts and modellers rerun the same inputs and trace results to exact data and code.

en.title: Big data and distributed computing
en.short: Why and how to spread storage and computation across many machines, with MapReduce and Spark.

sections.heading: When tools are needed
sections.text: Big-data tools are needed when a dataset is too large for one machine’s memory or disk, or a computation on one machine would take too long. They are not needed when the data fits comfortably and the job finishes quickly. The costs are real: clusters are expensive, network transfer is slow compared with local disk, and distributed programs are harder to write and debug. A single powerful machine is often simpler and cheaper.

sections.heading: Storage and partitioning
sections.text: Distributed storage splits a file into blocks and places them on many machines. Each block is stored on several machines, commonly three, so a lost machine does not lose data. Partitioning decides which records go to which machine. Range partitioning sends ordered ranges to different nodes; hash partitioning sends a record to a node by a hash of its key. Good partitioning balances the work. Data locality means running computation on the machine that holds the data, avoiding network transfer.

sections.heading: Fault tolerance
sections.text: In a large cluster, disk and machine failures are normal, not exceptional. Fault tolerance means the job still finishes. Replication protects stored data. For computation, a system can rerun lost tasks. MapReduce writes intermediate results to disk, so it can recover after a failure. Spark records the lineage, the sequence of transformations, so it can recompute lost partitions.

sections.heading: MapReduce and Spark
sections.text: MapReduce has map, shuffle and reduce phases. Mappers process blocks in parallel; the shuffle groups values by key across the network; reducers aggregate. The shuffle is often the bottleneck. Spark keeps data in memory and plans a directed acyclic graph of stages, which is faster for iterative work. Example: a 1 TB file read at 100 MB/s takes 1,000,000 ÷ 100 = 10,000 s, about 2.8 hours on one disk. Split over 100 machines, each reads 10 GB, or 100 s, before overheads.

keyPoints: Use distributed tools only when data or computation exceeds one machine; clusters add cost and complexity.
Distributed storage splits data into replicated blocks, and partitioning assigns records to nodes.
Fault tolerance comes from replication and from recomputing lost tasks.
MapReduce uses map, shuffle and reduce phases; the shuffle moves data across the network.
Spark keeps data in memory and uses lineage to recompute lost partitions.
A 1 TB file at 100 MB/s takes 10,000 s on one disk and about 100 s on 100 machines before overheads.

en.title: Deep learning foundations
en.short: This summary covers neural networks, activations, losses, backpropagation, training, regularisation, CNNs and RNNs.

sections.heading: Network structure
sections.text: A neural network is layers of units. The input layer holds the features. Each unit computes z = Σ(w × x) + b, then an activation a = f(z). Weights w and bias b are learned parameters. A feedforward network passes data from input to output; depth means more layers. The output layer matches the task: one linear unit for regression, a sigmoid unit for binary classification, or softmax for several classes.

sections.heading: Activation and loss
sections.text:
Activation functions add non-linearity. ReLU, f(z)=max(0,z), is common and cheap. Sigmoid maps to (0,1); softmax turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1. Without non-linearity, stacked layers collapse to one linear map. A loss function scores predictions against targets. Mean squared error suits regression; cross-entropy suits classification.

Worked example: x=(1,2), w=(0.5,0.5), b=−0.5, target y=3. z=1×0.5+2×0.5−0.5=1.0, a=ReLU(1)=1. Squared loss L=0.5(a−y)²=0.5(1−3)²=2.

sections.heading: Backpropagation and training
sections.text: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to find each parameter’s gradient of the loss. For the example, dL/da=a−y=−2, da/dz=1, so dL/dw1=−2×1=−2 and dL/dw2=−2×2=−4. Gradient descent updates w = w − r × dL/dw, where r is the learning rate. Training splits data into batches; one full pass through the data is an epoch, and training repeats for several epochs. A rate too large can diverge; too small learns slowly.

sections.heading: Regularisation and architectures
sections.text: Overfitting means low training loss but poor new-data performance. Regularisation limits it: weight decay adds a penalty on large weights, dropout randomly disables units during training, early stopping ends training when validation loss rises, and data augmentation creates altered copies. Convolutional networks apply small shared filters to local patches, then pool, which suits images. Recurrent networks keep a hidden state across time steps, which suits sequences; gated variants such as LSTM (long short-term memory) and GRU (gated recurrent unit) reduce vanishing gradients.

keyPoints: A unit computes z = Σ(w × x) + b and outputs a = f(z).
ReLU, sigmoid and softmax are common activation functions; non-linearity is essential.
Mean squared error is used for regression and cross-entropy for classification.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute gradients, and gradient descent updates weights by w = w − r × dL/dw.
Regularisation methods such as weight decay, dropout and early stopping reduce overfitting.
CNNs use shared convolutional filters for images; RNNs keep a hidden state for sequences.

en.title: Data visualisation and communication
en.short: Matching charts to questions, uncertainty, dashboards, accessibility, and presenting results to different audiences.

sections.heading: Choosing charts
sections.text: Match the chart to the question. A bar chart compares values across categories; a line chart shows change over time; a scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables; a histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable. Use a pie chart only for parts of a single whole with few slices. Label axes with units, state the sample size, and avoid decorative 3D effects. For non-technical readers, choose the simplest chart and add a one-sentence takeaway.

sections.heading: Showing uncertainty
sections.text: Every estimate has uncertainty. Show it with error bars or shaded bands, which mark a range of plausible values, and say in the caption what they represent. Do not hide uncertainty by plotting only a mean. In a small clinic case, waits of 10, 12, 15, 20 and 60 minutes give a median of 15 minutes but a mean of 23.4 minutes; the long wait pulls the mean up. A dot plot or box plot shows the uneven spread better than a single average. Avoid false precision: round to the data’s accuracy.

sections.heading: Dashboards and access
sections.text: A dashboard is a screen that answers a focused question with a few linked charts. Design one main question per dashboard, put the most important number first, show definitions and the update time, and remove clutter. Accessibility means people with different abilities can use the work. Use readable fonts, strong contrast, colour-blind safe palettes, direct labels, and alt text, a short written description of an image. Follow current Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Test with a keyboard and screen reader.

sections.heading: Presenting results
sections.text: For a written report, lead with the answer, then the evidence, then the method. State limits and do not imply causation without a suitable design. For an oral talk, give one message per slide, explain each technical term the first time, and rehearse the ending. For technical readers, include model details and checks in an appendix. For non-technical readers, use plain words, a concrete example and a clear recommendation. Invite questions and answer without overclaiming.

keyPoints: Match the chart to the question: bar for category comparison, line for time, scatter for relationships, histogram for distribution.
Show uncertainty with error bars or bands and explain them in the caption.
For skewed data, report the median and show the distribution, not only the mean.
A dashboard should answer one focused question and show definitions and update time.
Make charts accessible with contrast, colour-blind safe palettes, direct labels and alt text.
In reports and talks, lead with the answer, define terms, and separate technical detail for technical readers.

en.title: Ethics, privacy and data governance
en.short: Consent, fairness, privacy, data protection, transparency and accountability in data work.

sections.heading: Informed consent
sections.text: Informed consent means telling people in plain language what data you will collect, why, who will see it, the risks, and that they may refuse or withdraw without penalty. Consent must be voluntary and given with capacity. For children or vulnerable people, a guardian may need to agree. If the purpose changes, ask again. Record what was agreed and when.

sections.heading: Bias and fairness
sections.text: Bias is a systematic error that pushes results in one direction. It can enter through who is sampled, how labels are recorded, or proxy variables such as postcode standing in for income. A model can be accurate overall yet fail a group. Fairness has several meanings, including equal accuracy, equal error rates, or equal outcomes. These can conflict, so state your definition. Test performance by group and document gaps.

sections.heading: Privacy and protection
sections.text: Privacy is a person’s control over how their information is used. Personal data is any information that can identify a person, directly or indirectly. Data protection law sets duties for handling it. Common principles include lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation, security and individual rights. Pseudonymisation replaces names with codes but may still allow re-identification; anonymisation must be strong. Access control, encryption and retention rules reduce harm. Laws differ by country, for example the EU GDPR and Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023; check the current official source.

sections.heading: Transparency and governance
sections.text: Transparency means explaining data sources, model logic, limitations and decisions in language users can understand. Accountability means named people and bodies answer for compliance and harms. Data governance is the set of policies, roles and controls for access, quality, retention and incident response. Keep an audit trail and review models after deployment. Professional codes vary, so check the current code for your country and field. Case: a Lagos clinic uses an app to predict missed appointments. Staff explain the purpose, ask consent, allow opt out, and test whether the model works as well for patients without smartphones. They record approval and review yearly.

keyPoints: Informed consent must be voluntary, specific, understood and recorded, and renewed if the purpose changes.
Bias can enter through sampling, labels and proxies; test model performance by group.
Fairness definitions can conflict, so state and justify the one you use.
Personal data includes indirect identifiers; apply data minimisation, security and retention limits.
Transparency explains sources, logic and limits; accountability names who answers for harms.
Data protection laws and professional codes vary by country and change, so check current official sources.

en.title: Data science project lifecycle and capstone
en.short: Framing, planning, deployment, monitoring, documentation and a capstone workflow for data science projects.

sections.heading: Framing and requirements
sections.text:
Problem framing turns a vague request into a decision and a measurable goal. Name the decision maker, the action the project will change, the users and the success metric. State constraints too: data access, budget, staff skills, deadlines and legal duties.

Requirements list what the system must do (functional) and how well (non-functional), such as accuracy, latency, privacy and cost. Write each one so it can be tested; an untestable wish is not a requirement.

sections.heading: Planning and constraints
sections.text:
Project planning breaks the work into stages with owners, milestones and a realistic timeline. List risks: late data, missing values, blocked access, staff turnover and a model no one will maintain. Plan for version control, storage and compute costs.

Organisational constraints decide what is possible: a hospital may not move patient data to a public cloud, and a small retailer may have no engineer to run a live service. Build slack for approvals and cleaning.

sections.heading: Deployment and monitoring
sections.text:
Deployment puts the work into use. Choose batch scoring, a dashboard, an API or a scheduled report by how often decisions are made. Test with real users, keep a rollback plan, and record model and data versions.

Monitoring checks that the system still works: input data drift, missing fields, latency, cost and decision quality. Set alerts and a review schedule. A model that is never retrained or checked will decay. Decide who owns the service and what triggers a retrain.

sections.heading: Capstone and documentation
sections.text:
Documentation is part of the product: a data dictionary, a model card, a runbook and a report stating the question, data, method, results and limits. A capstone applies the full workflow.

Suppose Amina, an analyst at a Nigerian retailer, must reduce stock-outs. She frames the weekly reorder decision, writes requirements, plans around a slow supplier feed, builds and evaluates a forecast, then writes a deployment and monitoring plan. The defence explains trade-offs to a non-technical panel.

keyPoints: Frame the project as a decision with a measurable success metric and named users.
Requirements must be testable and cover both functional and non-functional needs.
Plan for risks, data access, costs and the organisation’s real constraints.
Deployment needs a rollback plan, version records and a chosen delivery mode.
Monitor data drift, performance, cost and decision quality, and set a retraining trigger.
A capstone should document the full workflow and defend its trade-offs, including to non-technical stakeholders.

en.title: Advanced statistical learning
en.short: Regularisation, support vector machines, ensembles, high-dimensional selection and their trade-offs.

sections.heading: Regularisation
sections.text:
Regularisation adds a penalty to the loss to control model complexity. Ridge minimises RSS + λΣβ_j² and has closed form β = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy; it keeps all coefficients. Lasso minimises RSS + λΣ|β_j| and can set some coefficients exactly to zero, so it selects variables. λ is chosen by cross-validation.

Example: with x = (1, 2), y = (2, 4), through-origin ridge gives β = Σxy ÷ (Σx² + λ) = 10 ÷ (5 + 5) = 1 when λ = 5; OLS gives 2.

sections.heading: Margins and kernels
sections.text: A support vector machine finds the separating hyperplane with the largest margin. The soft-margin objective minimises ½||w||² + CΣξ_i subject to y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 − ξ_i, ξ_i ≥ 0. C controls the cost of violations: large C fits training data closely, small C allows more margin errors. Kernels replace dot products with K(x_i, x_j), giving nonlinear boundaries without explicit coordinates. Linear SVMs are interpretable; kernel SVMs are less so.

sections.heading: Ensembles and boosting
sections.text: Bagging averages models fitted to bootstrap samples and mainly reduces variance; random forests add random feature selection. Boosting fits weak learners sequentially, each to the current residuals or errors, and adds them with a small learning rate ν: F_m = F_{m−1} + ν f_m. It mainly reduces bias. Gradient boosting generalises to any differentiable loss. Ensembles often predict well but are harder to interpret; feature importance is a rough guide.

sections.heading: High dimensions and trade-offs
sections.text: When predictors p exceed observations n, ordinary least squares is unstable or undefined. Selection methods include subset selection, lasso and elastic net; validate on held-out data. Ridge assumes dense linear effects; lasso assumes sparsity; SVMs need a suitable kernel; ensembles need useful weak learners. Theory separates approximation error, estimation error and noise: more flexibility lowers bias but raises variance. The curse of dimensionality makes local methods unreliable as p grows. No method wins everywhere (no free lunch). Choose by assumptions, interpretability and measured predictive performance.

keyPoints: Ridge minimises RSS + λΣβ_j² and shrinks coefficients; lasso minimises RSS + λΣ|β_j| and can select variables.
The ridge closed form is β = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy; λ is tuned by cross-validation.
A soft-margin SVM minimises ½||w||² + CΣξ_i subject to y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 − ξ_i, ξ_i ≥ 0.
Kernels let an SVM learn nonlinear boundaries by replacing inner products with K(x_i, x_j).
Bagging and random forests mainly reduce variance; boosting adds weak learners sequentially and mainly reduces bias.
High-dimensional selection needs regularisation and validation; flexibility trades bias against variance, and no method is best everywhere.

en.title: Bayesian inference and probabilistic modelling
en.short: Priors, likelihoods, posteriors, MCMC, hierarchical models and probabilistic programming.

sections.heading: Bayes and uncertainty
sections.text:
Bayesian inference treats an unknown quantity as a random variable with a probability distribution. Before seeing data, that distribution is the prior. The likelihood is the probability of the observed data given the parameter. Bayes’ theorem combines them: posterior ∝ prior × likelihood. The posterior is the updated distribution, so uncertainty is shown by its spread, not only by a point estimate. A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with posterior probability 0.95, given the model and prior.

Example: a conversion rate p has prior Beta(2,2), mean 0.5. In 10 visits there are 7 conversions. The binomial likelihood gives posterior Beta(2+7, 2+3) = Beta(9,5). Its mean is 9 ÷ 14 = 0.643, between the prior mean and the sample proportion 0.7.

sections.heading: Computing the posterior
sections.text: Conjugate priors give closed-form posteriors, as the beta-binomial example does. Otherwise the normalising constant is often intractable. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws a dependent sequence of parameter values whose long-run distribution is the posterior. Metropolis-Hastings proposes a move and accepts it with probability min(1, posterior ratio × proposal ratio). Good chains need convergence checks and may discard early burn-in draws. Variational inference is a faster approximation that replaces sampling with optimisation.

sections.heading: Hierarchical models
sections.text: A hierarchical model gives parameters their own distribution. For students grouped in schools, each school has an effect drawn from a common normal distribution. This shares information across groups, called partial pooling. Groups with little data are pulled towards the overall mean; groups with much data stay close to their own estimates. The cost is more parameters and more careful checking.

sections.heading: Probabilistic programming
sections.text: Probabilistic programming writes a model as code: priors, likelihood and dependencies. An inference engine then runs MCMC or variational inference. This makes complex models easier to build and check, but the engine’s diagnostics still matter. Always check prior sensitivity, convergence and posterior predictive fit.

keyPoints: Bayes’ theorem: posterior ∝ prior × likelihood.
For a Beta(a,b) prior with s successes and f failures, the posterior is Beta(a+s, b+f).
In the example, Beta(2,2) with 7 successes and 3 failures gives Beta(9,5), mean 9 ÷ 14 = 0.643.
MCMC samples from a posterior that has no closed form; check convergence and burn-in.
Hierarchical models use partial pooling, so small groups borrow strength from the whole.
Probabilistic programming separates model code from the inference engine, but diagnostics remain essential.

en.title: Advanced deep learning
en.short: Transformers, generative models, representation learning, optimisation and evaluation of deep models.

sections.heading: Transformers
sections.text:
A transformer reads a whole sequence at once. In self-attention each token is projected into a query, key and value vector, and its output is a weighted sum of values, with weights from softmax(QKᵀ ÷ √d). Multi-head attention repeats this in parallel; layers add residual connections and layer normalisation. Strengths: long-range dependencies and parallel training on GPUs. Failure mode: cost grows with the square of sequence length.

Example: n = 1,000 tokens, d = 512. The score matrix has n² = 1,000,000 entries, and the main products cost about 2n²d = 2 × 1,000,000 × 512 ≈ 1.02 × 10⁹ operations per head per layer, so 8 heads × 12 layers ≈ 1.0 × 10¹¹.

sections.heading: Generative models
sections.text: Generative models learn a data distribution so they can sample new items. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) train an encoder and decoder on a lower bound on likelihood. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) train a generator against a discriminator. Diffusion models learn to reverse gradual noise addition and give strong image quality. Autoregressive models predict the next token. Failure modes: VAEs give blurry samples, GANs can collapse, diffusion sampling is slow.

sections.heading: Representation learning
sections.text: Representation learning trains a model to map raw inputs to vectors that make later tasks easy. Self-supervised learning builds a task from unlabelled data, such as masking words and predicting them, or contrasting two views of an image. Transfer learning then fine-tunes the pretrained model on a small labelled set. Risk: the features carry the biases of the source data.

sections.heading: Optimisation and evaluation
sections.text:
Adam adapts a step size per parameter; learning-rate schedules and warm-up often matter more than the optimiser. Regularisers include weight decay, dropout, early stopping, augmentation and label smoothing. Evaluate on held-out data, over several seeds, with metrics that match deployment.

Example: chest X-ray classifiers that score highly in-house have repeatedly dropped several AUC points on images from hospitals outside their training data, because scanners and patient populations differ.

keyPoints: Self-attention weights come from softmax(QKᵀ ÷ √d), and cost grows as O(n²d) per layer.
Diffusion models currently lead image generation; GANs sample fast but can collapse.
Self-supervised pretraining then fine-tuning is the standard route when labels are scarce.
Adam with a warm-up schedule is a safe default optimiser for transformers.
Weight decay, dropout, early stopping and augmentation reduce overfitting but cannot fix biased data.
Report results over several seeds and on data from the deployment setting; in-house scores often overstate field performance.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation
en.short: Planning, conducting and defending an independent data science research project.

sections.heading: Research design
sections.text: A research design is the plan that links your question to evidence. Start with a focused question and, where appropriate, a testable hypothesis. Choose a design: experimental, observational, survey, case study or simulation. State your population, sampling method, variables and analysis plan. A literature review is not a list of papers. It is a critical synthesis: search systematically, record inclusion and exclusion criteria, compare findings, and identify the gap your project fills. For example, Ada studies mobile-money fraud in Nigeria. Her question asks which transaction features predict fraud. Her design uses a retrospective sample of anonymised records, and her review shows that earlier studies rarely include agent location.

sections.heading: Ethics, data and reproducibility
sections.text: Ethics approval is permission from your institution’s ethics committee (sometimes called an IRB) before you collect or use data involving people. Requirements vary by institution and country; check yours early. A data management plan (DMP) states what data you will collect, how you will store it, who can access it, how long you will keep it, and how you will protect personal data under the law in your country. Reproducibility means another researcher can obtain your results from the same data and code. Keep raw data unchanged, document cleaning steps, use version control, and record software versions. Replicability means new data give the same conclusions.

sections.heading: Writing and defending
sections.text: Academic writing in a dissertation is structured and evidence-based. Typical sections are introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion. Write in plain, precise English; define terms; report limitations honestly. The dissertation presentation, often an oral defence or viva voce, requires a short talk and answers to examiners. Prepare slides that show the question, method, key results and contribution. Rehearse the three-minute summary. In Ada’s case, she would explain her sampling, her ethics approval, her DMP, and why her model’s performance is credible.

keyPoints: A research design links a focused question to a sampling and analysis plan.
A literature review synthesises sources and identifies the gap, not just summarises them.
Ethics approval is needed before you collect or use data about people; rules vary by institution and country.
A data management plan covers storage, access, retention and legal protection of data.
Reproducibility needs unchanged raw data, documented code and recorded software versions.
A dissertation defence (viva voce) tests your method, results and contribution.
